paper_topic: Backtracking via a special [RESET] token lets language models undo and recover from their own unsafe generations during SFT/DPO training

nodes.text: Remarkable progress has been recently made in building capable and helpful large language models (Touvron et al., 2023).
As capabilities become more powerful, these models also have more potential to cause real societal harms (Kumar et al., 2023).
nodes.display_label: more capability brings more harm potential

nodes.text: The de facto standard in safety alignment focuses on prevention: training language models to generate safe responses while minimizing the likelihood of unsafe ones, through techniques including SFT (Ouyang et al., 2022) and RLHF (Christiano et al., 2017).

Prevention-based safety tuning goes a long way towards building safe language models (Bai et al., 2022a), and yet the safety of production models which have undergone substantial safety tuning (e.g., Claude 3.5 and GPT-4) can still be compromised in the wild by simple attacks (Andriushchenko et al., 2024).
nodes.display_label: prevention helps but production models still broken

nodes.text: The core challenge of safety alignment seems to be that the attack surface induced by a text interface is practically infinite, and model developers have to rely on the generalization of safe behavior from a relatively small (often predominantly in English) safety tuning dataset to prevent every failure case.
nodes.display_label: attack surface infinite, tuning data small

nodes.text: To illustrate just how big this attack surface truly is, two recent papers jailbreak GPT-4 by encoding malicious instructions in base64 (Wei et al., 2023) and in low-resource languages such as Zulu (Yong et al., 2024).
It is plausible that, through pre-training, GPT-4 picked up capabilities to understand a variety of encodings and languages, but that safety tuning failed to cover these "edge" cases.
In this work, we ask: how can we meaningfully improve language model safety, given that models will likely always produce some unsafe generations?
nodes.display_label: research question: improve safety despite unsafe generations

nodes.text: We hypothesize that it can be easier for a model to verify safety after some tokens have been generated, instead of relying on prevention of unsafe generations solely.
nodes.display_label: hypothesis: post-hoc verification easier than prevention

nodes.text: To this end, we introduce backtracking, a technique that allows language models to verify and "undo" prior unsafe generations and start anew.
Specifically, we allow language models to emit a special token, [RESET], upon which the generation API discards tokens prior to [RESET].

During training, we supervise language models to properly backtrack by constructing contrastive safety demonstrations, generations that are initially unsafe, but then backtrack into a fresh, safe response (e.g., Here is a vile letter [RESET] Sorry I cannot help with that.)

Our findings demonstrate that incorporating off-the-shelf alignment techniques, such as SFT and DPO, with our proposed backtracking method substantially improves the safety of both Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3-8B models.
Notably, this improvement in safety does not come at the cost of reduced model utility.
When a language model backtracks, it produces tokens that are not useful to the user, which decreases generation efficiency.

We find that this tradeoff between safety and efficiency due to backtracking can be simply adjusted using logit bias, and discover that large safety gains can be achieved with minimal impact on generation efficiency.
Finally, we evaluate our models against three state-of-the-art adversarial attacks (e.g., GCG (Zou et al., 2023b)), in addition to an adaptive attack designed to break backtracking.
nodes.display_label: evaluate vs 3 SOTA attacks + adaptive attack

nodes.text: Against every attack that we have tried, backtracking improves model safety over the baseline despite not being adversarially trained.
nodes.display_label: improves safety on every attack tested

observations:
The Backtracking intro shows a longer, more nuanced Prior_Work / Limitation spine than typical AI-paper templates. It opens with a two-sentence Context (LLM progress + harms), then one Prior_Work node naming the prevention paradigm (SFT/RLHF), then a second Prior_Work node that already begins to qualify the paradigm ('goes a long way... and yet... can still be compromised'). This 'and yet' is a rhetorical pivot but the sentence is structurally a Prior_Work assessment, not yet evaluative critique.

The Limitation band is unusually long: four nodes cover (i) the 'practically infinite' attack-surface diagnosis, (ii) two concrete jailbreak examples (base64 + Zulu), (iii) the inferential gap between pretraining-acquired capabilities and tuning coverage, and (iv) the framing research question itself. Real-paper signal: the gap is built up empirically rather than asserted in a single 'However' sentence.

The Method band moves through hypothesis → named technique → mechanism ([RESET] token) → training procedure (contrastive demonstrations) — four nodes rather than the typical bullet-list compression.

The Result band is wide (six nodes) and contains an internal contrast: N14 (no utility regression) is followed by N15 ('When a language model backtracks, it produces tokens that are not useful... decreases generation efficiency') — a frank tradeoff disclosure rather than a contribution puff. N16 then resolves it via logit bias, and N17-N18 add an adversarial-attack robustness pair.

Notably this paper has NO Contribution-band node — the introduction ends on Result/Robustness rather than a labeled contribution list. Two cross-band addresses edges: the backtracking method (N10) addresses the 'infinite attack surface / small tuning set' limitation (N5) and the 'edge cases not covered by safety tuning' limitation (N7). Both share the distinctive 'safety / unsafe generations / attack' lexical anchor and target the specific gaps that motivated the method.
